fullContent: Answers の BookletCh10 - 13 MetalsMetal Corrosion(Part 4) Metal Corrosion’s definitions (HKDSE Syllabus)Corrosion —- Natural process where a refined metal degrades due to a chemical reaction with its environment (usually turning the metal surface into an oxide) Rusting —- Common term for corrosion of iron to form hydrated iron(III) oxide (mixture)Conductive medium —- Materials that allow the flow of electric charge Electrolytes —- Substances have a natural positive or negative electrical charge when dissolved in H2OCorrosion resistance —- The ability of a material to resist degradation caused by chemical or electrochemical reactions with the environment (such as oxidation). Metal Corrosion and Rusting (HKDSE Syllabus)🔑 Key PhrasesCorrosionNatural process where a refined metal degrades due to a chemical reaction with its environment which usually turns the metal surface into an oxide.RustingCommon term for corrosion of iron to form hydrated iron(III) oxide (mixture).📌 Major PointsNature of rusting Hydrated Iron (III) oxide / Fe2O3 ᐧ xH2O , which is a compound 4Fe + 3O2 + 2xH2O → 2Fe2O3 . xH2O (4322 v.s. 5422)CriteriaWater Air (oxygen) 👣 Baby StepsWhy metal corrosion?For a corroding metal, its metal atoms on the surface change into metal ions,and a surface coating is formed (i.e. metal oxide). The coating often flakes off or is porous to both air and waterWhy no rusting?H2O and air (oxygen) are the criteria of rusting If ❰ * ❱, ❰ H2O / O2 ❱ will be removed. Thus, the iron will not rust 🤟Show FlatWhy is there metal corrosion? (2 marks)For a corroding metal, its metal atoms on the surface change into metal ions,and a surface coating is formed (usually a metal oxide). The coating often flakes off or is porous to both air and waterCan Fe be rust when placed in a desiccator? (2 marks)No, since H2O and air (oxygen) are the criteria of rusting If place the Fe in a desiccator, H2O will be removed. Thus, the iron will not rust Factor of facilitating Rusting (HKDSE Syllabus)📌 Major PointsFactorsPresent of ionic substances, ∵ Electrolyte can facilitate the transfer of electrons and ionsHigh temperatures, ∵ Provide more kinetic energy to the particle which can transfer electrons more readily On sharp or bent surface, ∵ Increase its surface area per unit volume so more chemicals can react with Fe Attachment to a less reactive metal, ∵ More reactive metal will lose electrons more readily Present of nitrogen oxide, ∵ Strong oxidizing agent 🤟Show FlatHow can I speed up rusting? Explain Briefly. (2 marks)Adding NaCl (aq) in Fe, since NaCl (aq) is an electrolyte which can facilitate the transfer of electrons and ions (Or other suitable answers) Observation in Rustinwsg (HKDSE Syllabus)🔑 Key PhrasesPotassium hexacyanoferrate (III) K3[Fe(CN6)]Form blue colour due to the formation of Fe2+ ionsPhenolphthalein C2oH14O4Form pink colour due to the formation of OH- ions📌 Major PointsRust indicatorFormed by potassium hexacyanoferrate (III) and phenolphthalein K3[Fe(CN6)] / C20H14O4 Rusting regionFor Blue colour (K3[Fe(CN)6]) : Head and tip & The region with anglesFor Pink colour (C20H14O4) : Body part👣 Baby StepsNo rusting There is pink colour formed onlySince there are formation of OH- ions onlyThis indicate no rusting occur RustingThere are both blue and pink colour formed / There is blue colour formedSince there are formation of Fe2+ and OH- ions / Fe2+ ions only This indicate rusting occur Why in gel form?Provide a medium for ion movement But to prevent the spread of the colour of the indicator 🤟Show FlatWhy is the rust indicator usually in gel form ? (1 mark)Provide a medium for ion movement But to prevent the spread of the colour of the indicator Preventive measure 1 : Protective coating (HKDSE Syllabus)📌 Major PointsPrincipleBy preventing Fe contact with water and air (oxygen)FeaturesInvolve coating Preventing Fe contact with water and air (oxygen)For Tin-plating & Galvanizing : Tin will cause rust more severe while Zn will still protect Fe For Tin-plating & Galvanizing : Tin cause rust faster while Zn slower when coating is scrapped off For Galvanizing : Acting both sacrificial protection and Protective coating protection MaterialExample Reasons of (not) using itPHYPaint 油漆 BridgeshipOther larger objectPrevent rusting (major)Good appearence ✅Pollute air ❌PHYOiling / Greasing 油Industrial machinery(Libricant)Other larger objectPrevent rusting (major)Act as a lubricant ✅Require high condition in temperature❌PHYPlasticing 塑料FilmOther larger objectPrevent rusting (major)Good corrosion resistance ✅Low melting point ❌CHEM/PHYGalvanizing/Zinc-plating 鍍鋅Roofs BucketsPrevent rusting (major)Still protect Fe when the coating is damaged ✅Zn2+ ions is toxic ❌CHEM/PHYTin-plating 鍍錫 Food cansPrevent rusting (major)Tin ions is non-toxic ✅Fe rust more severe when the coating is damaged ❌CHEMElectroplating(Cr/Ni)電鍍 Bathroom fittings Car bumpersPrevent rusting (major)Good appearence ✅Cr is expensive ❌👣 Baby StepsWhy rusting more severe?After the tin-plating is scrapped off, it no longer protects the Fe and Tn is less reactive than Feso that Fe will contact O2 and water and lose e- more readily. Thus rusting is more severe Preventive measure 2 : Cathodic Protection (HKDSE Syllabus)📌 Major PointsPrincipleBy supplying e- to Fe from the negative terminal of a power supply in order to prevent the formation of Fe2+ ionsFeaturesInvolve supplying e- to FeInvolve connecting the iron to negative terminal of a power supply Preventing formation of Fe2+ ionsPhysical methodMaterialPlatinum / PtExamplesCar bodies Pipeline Water and fuel tank Preventive measure 3 : Sacrificial Protection (HKDSE Syllabus)📌 Major PointsPrincipleFe attach to a more reactive metal which will lose e- more readily than Fe to prevent the formation of Fe2+ ionsFeaturesInvolve Fe contact with a more reactive metal Involve the more reactive metal lose electron more readily than Fe Preventing formation of Fe2+ ionsChemical methodMaterialMagnesium (Mg) Zinc (Zn)ExamplesPipelineShips👣 Baby Steps#1 StructureSacrificial Protection❰ X ❱ are attached to Fe. ❰ X ❱ is sacrificed to protect Fe.❰ X ❱ are attached to Fe. ❰ X ❱ will corrode in preference to Fe. ❰ X ❱ are attached to Fe. ❰ X ❱ will lose e- more readily than Fe. (Any one of them)#2 General questionsWhy seldom use Ca under the sea?❰ X ❱ is very reactive metal, it will react with water.Why replaced regularly?Since ❰ Zn/Mg ❱ will be consumed, and it will no longer protect the Fe🤟Show FlatWhy do people seldom use Ca to protect the iron under the sea? (1 mark)Ca is very reactive metal, it will react with water.Why should Zn / Mg be replaced regularly with underground iron? (1 mark)Since Zn / Mg will be consumed, and it will no longer protect the Fe Preventive measure 4 : Alloying (HKDSE Syllabus)📌 Major PointsPrincipleAdd another atoms into Fe to prevent rustingFeaturesAdd another atoms into Fe to prevent rustingPhysical method MaterialChromium (Cr) Nickel (Ni)Manganese (Mn)ExamplesCookware Surgery Instrument keySteel Iron and carbonBronze Copper 88% and Tin (Sn) 12% Socioeconomic implications of rusting (HKDSE Syllabus)👣 Baby StepsWhy important to prevent rusting?Rusting affects the safety of using them and results in great economic loss.🤟Show FlatWhy is it important to prevent rusting? (1 mark)Rusting affects the safety of using them and results in great economic loss. (1 mark)Au is chemically inert and it will not react with water and airExplain whether Au or Al has a higher corrosion resistance. (3 marks)Au is chemically inert and it will not react with water and air.While Al has a protective layer (i.e. Al2O3) which stick firmly and impermeable to air and water only.Thus, Au has a higher corrosion resistance compare to Al Anodization of Aluminium (HKDSE Syllabus)📌 Major PointsPrincipleIncreasing the thickness of its oxides coating to increase its corrosion resistance, and surface hardness, and to allow dyeing more easilyDifferenceAnodization : increasing the thickness of its oxides coating (e.g. Al → Al2O3) and involve taking out the electrons.Electroplating : Adding a layer of different metal (e.g. gold)Cathodic Protection : Supplying electrons to prevent rusting ExamplesSoft drink cans Cooking pots Window frames (/ chocolate wrappings → Al foil ❌) Contents Page Page Metal Corrosion’ definitionsPage Metal Corrosion Page Factor to facilitate the rusting Page Observation in rustingPage Preventive Measure 1 : Protective Coating Page Preventive Measure 2 : Cathodic ProtectionPage Preventive Measure 3 : Sacrificial ProtectionPage Preventive Measure 4 : AlloyingPage Socioeconomic implications of RustingPage Corrosion resistancePage Aluminium Anodization

Reaction between Hydroxide and Acids (HKDSE Syllabus)📌Major PointsFormulaMOH (s) + H+ (aq) → Mx+ (aq) + H2O (l) ObservationHeat released Metal Hydroxide is dissolved to give a colourless solution Reaction between Oxide and Acids (HKDSE Syllabus)📌Major PointsFormulaMO (s) + 2H+ (aq) → Mx+ (aq) + H2O (l) ObservationHeat released Metal Oxide is dissolved to give a colourless solution Reaction between Carbonate and Acids (HKDSE Syllabus)📌Major PointsFormulaMOH (s) + H+ (aq) → Mx+ (aq) + H2O (l) ObservationEffervescence (i.e. a large amount of gas bubble formed)Metal Carbonate is dissolved to give a colourless solution Reaction between Hydrogencarbonate and Acids (HKDSE Syllabus)📌Major PointsFormulaMHCO3 (s) + H+ (aq) → Mx+ (aq) + H2O (l) ObservationEffervescence (i.e. a large amount of gas bubble formed)Metal Hydrogencarbonate is dissolved to give a colourless solution Reasons for reactions / observations (HKDSE Syllabus)👣Baby Steps①Why effervescence?( When ❰ acid ❱ dissolves in water, it will ionize and give H+ ions ) H+ in the ❰ acid ❱ will react with the ❰ X ❱ to give CO2 (g)Why inappropriate?❰ X ❱ is too corrosive (e.g. Concentrate NaOH)The reaction is highly exothermic (e.g. HCl + NaOH)There are no reaction (e.g. Cu + HCl)Why produce more gas?Reaction is exothermic and solubility of ❰ X ❱ decreases. Thus, more gas bubblesWhy excess sample?To ensure all acids are all reacted and prevent it contaminate ❰ X ❱Why not be dried by heating/in oven?❰ X ❱ will lose the water of crystallization (for hydrated compound)❰ X ❱ will react with air to form impurities How to know a reaction is finished?No more gas bubbles formed Insoluble salt does not dissolve anymore Why cold water instead of warm water? [1]Higher the temperature of ❰ X ❱, higher the solubility of ❰ X ❱Thus, using cold water can prevent the loss of product. Why cold water instead of warm water? [2]Reaction between ❰ X ❱ and ❰ Y ❱ is highly exothermic Using warm water may cause a more serve reaction🤟Show FlatHow should you know a reaction is finished? (1 mark)No more gas bubbles formed // Insoluble salt does not dissolve anymore Steps for dilution of acid (HKDSE Syllabus)👣 Baby StepsProcedureConcentrated acid should be diluted by adding it slowly to a large amount of cold water with stirring.Why not water to alkali?A large amount of heat will be released (i.e. exothermic reaction), causing the water to vaporize quickly and acidic mist will be formed and the solution may violently splash out of the container.Why cold water?It is a highly exothermic reaction🤟Show FlatJacky claims that cold water should be added into concentrate NaOH, do you argee? (2 mark)No, since a large amount of heat will be released (i.e. exothermic reaction), causing the water to vaporize quickly and acidic mist will be formed and the solution may violently splash out of the container. Role of water (HKDSE Syllabus)👣 Baby Steps#1 Acidic Properties Affecting Acidic Properties❰ Solvent ❱ (does not) contains water. ❰ X ❱ can(not) exhibit its acidic properties in the ❰ presence/absent ❱ of H2O.#2 ExperimentWhy tap funnel?By closing the tap, it can prevent any gas escaping from the tap funnel.Control the rate of addition of the acid to ❰ X ❱Why inverted funnel?Prevent sucking back of water into the flat-bottomed flask due to gas pressure difference🤟Show FlatWhat conclusion can you make about acidic properties of HCl (g) in NaCl (aq) / Hexane? (1 mark) #1 Acidic Properties No, since HCl (s) does not contain any mobile ions and delocalized electronsWhy can hydrochloride acid turn blue litmus paper to red? (2 marls) #1 Acidic Properties HCl (s) contain water. HCl (s) can exhibit its acidic properties in the presence of water Why do I need to use a tap funnel for adding the acid to NaCl (s)? (2 marks) #2 ExperimentBy closing the tap, it can prevent any gas escaping from the tap funnel.Control the rate of addition of the acid to NaClWays to collect H2 gas (HKDSE Syllabus)📌Major PointsFormulaM (s) + 2H+ (aq) → Mx+ (aq) + H2 (g) ObservationHeat released Metal is dissolved to give a colourless solution❰ X ❱ react with magnesium to give a white fume (H2)(Colour change)Requirement❰ X ❱ is less dense than air and water ❰ X ❱ is water-insoluble ❰ X ❱ occupies space 👣 Baby StepsWhy “POP” sound when placed near H2?The flame provides the energy for the hydrogen gas to react with oxygen from the air.How to test H2?Using a burning splint and having a pop soundHow to test O2?Relight a glowing splint 🤟Show FlatHow can I test if there is H2 gas or not? Thus, it is a non-renewable resource. Hydrocarbons (HKDSE Syllabus) 🔑 Key PhrasesHydrocarbonA compound consisting only of carbon atoms and hydrogen atoms.👣 Baby StepsWhy various b.p. in hydrocarbons?[4 marks structure]❰ Larger the molecular sizes, stronger the strength of Van der Waals’ forces and vice versaStraight-chain (Branched-chain) molecules has stronger (Weaker) the strength of Van der Waals’ forces ❱ Hydrocarbons have different molecular sizes and shapes, resulting ❰ … ❱Thus, there are various boiling points of hydrocarbonsWhy no combustion of hydrocarbons?Petroleum contains many useful fractions (e.g. feedstock to make chemicals) Burning it will destroy the chemicals’ complex molecular structures and wastes these valuable materials. 🤟Show FlatWhy are there various boiling points of hydrocarbons ? (2 marks)Since termination of addition polymerization is a random chain-growth process. During the reaction, different polymer chains terminate at different times. This results in a mixture of polystyrene molecules with varying chain length.Thus, it only has an average molecular mass rather than a fixed one. the wedge and dash form a umbrella base at the bottom), Bond angle : < 109.5o]Trigonal bipyramidalIn total 5 e- clouds at central atom[1 wedge 1 dash 3 straight lines (1 vert. st. line up, 1 hor. st. line to the side. 1 Wedge → SW, dotted → NW), Bond angle : 90o/ 120o]Octa-hedralIn total 6 e- clouds at central atom[2 wedge 2 dash 2 straight lines(1 vert. st. line up, 1 hor. st. line to the side. 2 Wedge → SW/SE, 2 dotted → NW/NE), Bond angle : 90o/120o/180o]** SO2 ** Umbrella shape : 👣 Baby StepsMolecules do not follow octet rule No, since ❰ X ❱ is an [electron-deficient molecule / extended octet]The central atom of ❰ X ❱ (i.e. …) has an electronic arrangement of ❰ * ❱. It has ❰ * ❱ valence electrons in its outermost shell.By sharing its ❰ * ❱ valence electrons with ❰ Y ❱ atoms to form ❰ * ❱ single covalent bonds, the central ❰ * ❱ atom has a total of ❰ * ❱ electrons (i.e. ❰ * ❱ lone pairs & ❰ * ❱ bond pairs) surrounding it. Since this is [fewer/more] than 8 electrons, it does not follow the octet structure.Molecules follow octet rule Yes, since The central atom of ❰ X ❱ (i.e. …) has an electronic arrangement of ❰ * ❱. It has ❰ * ❱ valence electrons in its outermost shell.By sharing its ❰ * ❱ valence electrons with ❰ Y ❱ atoms to form ❰ * ❱ single covalent bonds, the central ❰ * ❱ atom has a total of 8 electrons surrounding it. Since this is equal to 8 electrons, it does follow the octet structure.Symmetrical and non-polar structureYes (No), since The attached atoms are the same (different) element and the central atom has no (contain) lone pairs.Thus, this structure can be said to be (a)symmetrical and (polar) non-polar🤟 Show FlatConsider the following species: CS2. It has 4 valence electrons in its outermost shell.By sharing its 4 valence electrons with 2 S atoms to form 2 double covalent bonds, the central carbon atom has a total of 8 electrons (i.e. 0 lone pairs & 4 bond pairs) surrounding it. content: Answers の BookletCh24 - 27 Microscopic World (II)Polarity of bond and molecule(Part 2) Definition of Polarity of bond and molecule (HKDSE Syllabus)Electronegativity of atoms —- The ability of the atom in a molecule to attract bonding electrons toward itself in a covalent bond.Polarity —- The property of having distinct, opposing poles or electrical charges due to an uneven distribution of electron density across a bond or a molecule.Polar Covalent Bond —- A covalent bond in which the bonding electron pair is shared unequally between two atoms due to an electronegativity differenceNon-polar Covalent Bond —- A covalent bond in which the bonding electron pair is shared equally between two atoms because they have zero or negligible electronegativity differenceElectron cloud —- Region of negative charge surrounding an atomic nucleus or a molecule where electrons are likely to be found.Dipole —- Separation of equal and opposite partial electric charges (δ+ & δ-) across a covalent bond or an entire molecule, caused by an unequal distribution of bonding electrons.Dipole moment —- Quantitative measure of the overall polarity of a molecule, representing the vector sum of all individual bond dipoles within that molecule. Electronegativity of atoms (HKDSE Syllabus) 🔑 Key PhrasesElectronegativityThe ability of the atom in a molecule to attract bonding electrons toward itself in a covalent bond.👣 Baby StepsPeriod’ trendCrossing from left to right, the nuclear charge increases steadily.
fullContent: Answers の BookletCh24 - 27 Microscopic World (II)Polarity of bond and molecule(Part 2) Definition of Polarity of bond and molecule (HKDSE Syllabus)Electronegativity of atoms —- The ability of the atom in a molecule to attract bonding electrons toward itself in a covalent bond.Polarity —- The property of having distinct, opposing poles or electrical charges due to an uneven distribution of electron density across a bond or a molecule.Polar Covalent Bond —- A covalent bond in which the bonding electron pair is shared unequally between two atoms due to an electronegativity differenceNon-polar Covalent Bond —- A covalent bond in which the bonding electron pair is shared equally between two atoms because they have zero or negligible electronegativity differenceElectron cloud —- Region of negative charge surrounding an atomic nucleus or a molecule where electrons are likely to be found.Dipole —- Separation of equal and opposite partial electric charges (δ+ & δ-) across a covalent bond or an entire molecule, caused by an unequal distribution of bonding electrons.Dipole moment —- Quantitative measure of the overall polarity of a molecule, representing the vector sum of all individual bond dipoles within that molecule. Electronegativity of atoms (HKDSE Syllabus) 🔑 Key PhrasesElectronegativityThe ability of the atom in a molecule to attract bonding electrons toward itself in a covalent bond.👣 Baby StepsPeriod’ trendCrossing from left to right, the nuclear charge increases steadily.This increase the electrons in the outermost shell, while the atomic radius decreases.Due to the higher effective nuclear charge and smaller atomic radius, the nucleus exerts a stronger electrostatic attraction on the bonding electron pair in a covalent bond. Group’ trendDecreasing down a group, the number of occupied electron shells increases steadily.This significantly increases the atomic radius and the number of inner-shell electrons.Due to the larger atomic radius and more number of inner-shell electrons, the nucleus exerts a weaker electrostatic attraction on the bonding electron pair in a covalent bond.🤟 Show FlatState the trend in electronegativity across Period 3 from sodium to chlorine. Explain the trend in terms of the structure of atoms. (3 marks)Crossing from left to right, the nuclear charge increases steadily.This increase the electrons in the outermost shell, while the atomic radius decreases as the outer shell is pulled closer to the nucleus.Due to the higher effective nuclear charge and smaller atomic radius, the nucleus exerts a stronger electrostatic attraction on the bonding electron pair in a covalent bond. Introduction of dipole, dipole moment and polarity (HKDSE Syllabus) 🔑 Key PhrasesPolarityUneven distribution of electrical charge across a molecule or a chemical bond.DipoleSeparation of equal and opposite partial electric charges (δ+ & δ-) across a covalent bond or an entire molecule, caused by an unequal distribution of bonding electrons.📌 Major PointsFactors affecting polarityElectronegativity DifferenceMolecular GeometryPresence of Lone Pairs Non-polar bond and non-polar molecule (HKDSE Syllabus) 📌 Major PointsNon-polar covalent moleculesWeak intermolecular forces, ∵ lack permanent dipoles, they cannot form permanent dipole-dipole interaction.Symmetrical shapeEqual Electron Sharing👣 Baby StepsWhy non-polar covalent bond ?The two atoms forming the bond (i.e. …) are the same element and possess zero electronegativity difference.Why non-polar molecule with polar Bonds ?The two atoms forming the bond (i.e. …) are the different elements and possess a electronegativity differenceWhile the ❰ X ❱ molecule possess a highly symmetrical ❰ shape ❱, the individual bond dipoles cancel each other out completely, leaving the overall molecule with no polarity.Why non-polar molecule ?The two atoms forming the bond (i.e. …) are the same element and possess zero electronegativity difference.The bonding electron cloud is shared equally between the two bonded atoms, resulting in overall molecule with no polarity.🤟 Show FlatExplain why the covalent bond in a homonuclear diatomic molecule, such as chlorine, is completely non-polar. (2 marks)The two atoms forming the bond (i.e. Cl-Cl) are the same element and possess zero electronegativity difference.The bonding electron cloud is shared equally between the two bonded atoms, resulting in overall molecule with no polarity.Tetrachloromethane contains four polar covalent bonds, yet it is classified as a non-polar molecule. Explain this phenomenon. (3 marks)The two atoms forming the bond (i.e. C-Cl) are the different elements and possess a electronegativity differenceWhile the CCl4 molecule possess a highly symmetrical Tetra-hedral shape, the individual bond dipoles cancel each other out completely, leaving the overall molecule with no polarity.Both carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide are triatomic molecules containing polar covalent bonds. Explain why CO2 is non-polar while SO2 is a polar molecule. (3 marks)The two atoms forming the bond (i.e. S=O and C=O) are the different elements and possess a electronegativity differenceWhile the CO2 molecule possess a highly symmetrical linear structure, the individual bond dipoles cancel each other out completely, leaving the overall molecule with no polarity.While the SO2 molecule possess a asymmetrical V-shape, the individual bond dipoles do not cancel each other out completely, leaving the overall molecule with polarity. Polar bond and polar molecule (HKDSE Syllabus) 📌 Major PointsDative covalent bondCovalent bond in which the bond pair of electrons is provided by only one of the bonding atoms👣 Baby StepsWhy polar covalent bond ?The two bonded atoms are different elements and have a difference in electronegativity. (i.e. The ❰ X ❱ is more electronegative than ❰ Y ❱) Since the bonding electron cloud is not shared equally, being pulled closer toward the ❰ X ❱This uneven sharing distorts the electron cloud, causing ❰ X ❱ to acquire a partial negative charge and ❰ Y ❱ to acquire a partial positive charge, establishing non-zero polarityWhy polar molecule ?The molecule has __ lone pair(s) in its outermost shell and thus __ polar ❰ X ❱ bonds are not on the same plane❰ X ❱ is not symmetrical / asymmetrical molecules and the polarity of the bonds do not cancel out each other.(Notes that a molecule can contain non-polar bonds and still be a polar molecule overall, e,g, CH4)🤟 Show FlatWith reference to electronegativity and electron cloud distribution, explain why a hydrogen chloride molecule possesses a permanent dipole. (3 marks)The two bonded atoms are different elements and have a difference in electronegativity. (The Cl is more electronegative than H) Since the bonding electron cloud is not shared equally, the bonding electron cloud is pulled closer toward the Cl atom.This uneven sharing distorts the electron cloud, causing Cl to acquire a partial negative charge and H to acquire a partial positive charge, establishing non-zero polarityExplain, from molecular level, why CH3F is polar. (1 marks)CH3F is asymmetrical molecules and the polarity of the bonds do not cancel out each other.Describe the polar bond formation between NH3 . (1 marks)The molecule has 1 lone pair(s) in its outermost shell and thus 3 polar N-H bonds are not on the same plane Liquid Jet Experiment (HKDSE Syllabus) 📌 Major PointsObservationPolar : Liquid jet is deflected towards the rodNon-poar : Liquid jet remains completely straight (No deflection)PrecautionEnsure there are no naked flames, ∵ Organic solvents are highly volatile and flammable.The charged rod can’t touch the liquid stream, ∵ Liquid stream will immediately stop deflecting and fall straight down👣 Baby StepsProcedureFill a clean, dry burette with the liquid to be tested Open the tap of the burette slightly to allow a thin, continuous, vertical stream (jet) of the liquid to run into a beaker below.Rub a polythene rod or a balloon vigorously with a piece of dry wool cloth to generate a static negative charge on its surface.Bring the charged rod close to—but not touching—the falling stream of liquid.Observe and record the result Classification of non-polar molecule and polar molecule (MC Skills) 📌 Major PointsClassificationLook at the central atom.If it has zero lone pairs and all attached atoms are identical ⇒ Non-polar moleculeIf the central atom has lone pairs or different attached atoms ⇒ Polar moleculeHydrocarbons are always non-polar in HKDSE syllabus 🤟Show FlatMC 1 O3 → Lone pair = (6-2)/2 = 2 ⇒ ❌ SiF4 → Lone pair = (4-4)/2 = 0 + Identical ⇒ ✅NF3 → Lone pair = (5-3)/2 = 1 ⇒ ❌CH2Cl2 → Lone pair = (4-4)/2 = 0 + different ⇒ ❌∴ B(Notes that all of them contain polar bonds)(For A, although it doesn’t have ΔEN, bonding)Which of the following molecules contains polar bonds but is a non-polar molecule overall?A. How VDW forces affects rate of evaporationEvaporation occurs when particles absorb heat from the surroundingsStronger (Weaker) intermolecular force in the liquid, the longer (shorter) time for the liquid to evaporate. 🤟Show FlatCompare the van der Waals’ forces between butane and butene. (2 marks)Both of them have a simple molecular structureButane has a similar molecular size with buteneThus, both of them have a similar strength of van der Waals' forces.Jacky said ‘The rate of evaporation of butane is higher than hexane.’ Justify his statement (3 marks)Both of them have a simple molecular structure while butane has a weaker van der Waals’ forces due to smaller molecular size than hexaneEvaporation occurs when particles absorb heat from the surroundingsStronger (Weaker) intermolecular force in the liquid, the longer (shorter) time for the liquid to evaporateThus, rate of evaporation of butane is higher than hexaneSuggest why Polyacrylonitrile (PAN) has a higher melting point than polyethene. (2 marks)The size of the PAN / nitrile group (−CN) is larger than a polyethene / hydrogen atom. The van der Waals’ forces between the PAN molecules are stronger than those between polyethene molecules. Thus, PAN has a higher melting point. There are ❰ * ❱ lone pairs of electrons on the ❰ N/O/F ❱ atom (only), but each ❰ * ❱ molecule has (only) ❰ * ❱ hydrogen atom.Thus, it can (only) form ❰ * ❱ hydrogen bond with other ❰ * ❱ molecules on average Drawing the formation of hydrogen bonding Draw the lewis structuresIdentify polarity (partial charges)Draw a dotted wedge directly from the partially positive hydrogen atom + From the electronDraw a straight line from the partially negative [F/O/N] atom 🤟Show FlatDescribe how hydrogen bonds form between water molecules. There are 2 lone pairs of electrons on the O atom, but each H2O molecule has 2 hydrogen atoms.Thus, it can form 2 hydrogen bond with other H2O molecules on averageWith the aid of a diagram, explain the formation of hydrogen bonding in hydrogen fluoride. Correct orientation of water molecules 1MCorrect labelling and position the hydrogen bond 1M Physical Properties 1 : Boiling point (HKDSE Syllabus) 📌 Major PointsFactor affecting boiling pointIntermolecular Forces Molecular Size Atmospheric Pressure👣 Baby Steps#1 Single comparison Backgroud ①All of them has a simple molecular structureVarious boiling point due to ΔENMore electronegative of an atom, the polarity of its bond is stronger.Thus, the van der Waals’ forces between its molecules are stronger, requiring more heat energy to overcome them.High boiling point due to hydrogen bondH is bonded to an highly electronegativity F atom HF has extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonds between moleculesHydrogen bond is stronger than van der Waals’ forceHF exhibits an extremely high boiling points #2 Multi-comparison Backgroud ①All of them has a simple molecular structureVarious in boiling point due to molecular size [For element & Compound with similar pattern]Increasing molecular mass has a greater chance to have electron cloud distortion Thus, stronger van der Waals' forces between separate molecules, requiring more heat energy to overcome the van der Waals' forces. Thus, the intermolecular forces between ❰ Z ❱ molecules are the weakest, requiring lowest heat energy to overcome them. Various in boiling point due to different polarity of bond[For non-polar / polar compound]Both ❰ X ❱ & ❰ Y ❱ are held by van der waals’ forces between their molecules respectivelyAs ❰ X ❱ is polar while ❰ Y ❱ is non-polar, ❰ X ❱ has a stronger van der waals’ forces between their molecules than those between ❰ Y ❱ molecules 🤟Show FlatWhy is the boiling point of Ar higher than the boiling point of Ne ? Resulting in higher boiling point than NeWith explanation, arrange the boiling point of H2O, F2, and H2 from the highest to lowest. (3 marks) #2 Multi-comparison Each H2O molecule can form 2 hydrogen bonds on averageBoth HF and NH3 has only has weak van der waals’ forces between their molecules, while F2 has a stronger van der waals’ forces than H2 (∵ larger molecular size in F2) Hydrogen bonds in the H2O molecule is much stronger than the van der waals’ forces between F2 and H2Thus, H2O > F2 > H2 A student said ‘ H2O molecules are polar while CH4 molecules are non-polar, resulting in a difference in boiling point’ Comment on the students statement. #2 Multi-comparison Incorrect, although both of them has simple molecular structure,H2O can form 2 hydrogen bonds on average which is stronger than the weak van der Waals’ forces between CH4 molecules.Thus, there are differences in boiling points instead of the polarity of the molecules. Physical Properties 2 : Surface tension (HKDSE Syllabus) 📌 Major PointsSurface tensionStrength of its intermolecular forces👣 Baby StepsComparison of surface tension❰ X ❱ has stronger intermolecular forces than ❰ Y ❱ due to ❰ Properites ❱ When the molecules of a liquid are attracted by stronger intermolecular forces, that liquid will have higher surface tension.Thus, ❰ X ❱ has a higher surface tension.🤟Show FlatWhy does water have a higher surface tension than many organic liquids ? (2 marks)H2O has stronger intermolecular forces than most organic liquid due to presence of extensive hydrogen bonding When the molecules of a liquid are attracted by stronger intermolecular forces, that liquid will have higher surface tension.Thus, H2O has a higher surface tension.Why does methanol have a higher surface tension than cyclohexane ? (2 marks)Methanol has stronger intermolecular forces than cyclohexane due to presence of extensive hydrogen bonding When the molecules of a liquid are attracted by stronger intermolecular forces, that liquid will have higher surface tension.Thus, Methanol has a higher surface tension. Physical Properties 3 : Viscosity (HKDSE Syllabus) 📌 Major PointsViscosityStrength of its intermolecular forcesTendency of molecules to become entangled with each other.👣 Baby StepsComparison of ViscosityThe number of hydrogen bonds formed per alcohol molecule on average is ❰ * ❱ for ❰ X ❱, ❰ * ❱ for ❰ Y ❱, ❰ * ❱ for ❰ Z ❱,So the intermolecular forces between the ❰ X ❱ and ❰ Z ❱ molecules is largest and smallest respectivelyThus, ❰ X ❱ has the highest viscosity and ❰ Z ❱ has the smallest viscosity 🤟Show FlatWith explanation, Arrange the viscosity of propan-1-ol, propane-1,2-diol, propane-1,2,3-triol in ascending order.The number of hydrogen bonds formed per alcohol molecule on average is one for propan-1-ol, two for propane-1,2-diol, three for propane-1,2,3-triolSo the intermolecular forces between the propane-1,2,3-triol molecules is largest and lowest in propan-1-olThus, propane-1,2,3-triol has the highest viscosity and propan-1-ol has the smallest viscosityPropan-1-ol > propane-1,2-diol > propane-1,2,3-triol Physical Properties 4 : Solubility (HKDSE Syllabus) 📌 Major PointsSolubilityTemperatureMolecular size and surface areaPressure👣 Baby StepsSingle of Solubility [Normal]Single of Solubility [With hydrogen bonding]❰ X ❱ can form hydrogen bonds with water and it is small enough.These attractions formed release enough energy to overcome the original forces and attractions (i.e. Hydrogen bond and chemical bond) holding the pure ❰ X ❱ particles together and the pure water particles together.Comparison of SolubilityThe hydroxyl groups in ❰ X ❱ can form hydrogen bonds with water.❰ Y ❱ is non-polar and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water.The weak van der Waals’ force between ❰ Y ❱ is insufficient to overcome the extensive hydrogen bonds between water molecules.Thus, ❰ X ❱ can dissolve in water while ❰ Y ❱ can’t 🤟Show FlatExplain why ammonia is soluble in water. (2 marks)NH3 can form hydrogen bonds with water and it is small enough.These attractions formed release enough energy to overcome the original forces and attractions (i.e. Hydrogen bond and chemical bond) holding the pure NH3 particles together and the pure water particles together.Explain why alcohol is miscible in water. Chemical cell v.s. Electrolytic cell (HKDSE Syllabus) 📌Major Points#1 DifferencesCells They have different FUNCTIONS. For Chemical cell, it generates electricity by redox reaction, while For Electrolytic cell, it drives a redox reaction by electricity.Their ENERGY CONSERVATIONS are different. For Chemical cell, it generates electricity by redox reaction, while For Electrolytic cell, it drives a redox reaction by electricity.They have different POLARITY OF ELECTRODES. For Chemical cell, its anode (cathode) is connected to negative (positive) electrode, while For Electrolytic cell, its anode (cathode) is connected to positive (negative)They have different TYPE OF REACTION. For Chemical cell, it has a spontaneous and exothermic reaction, while For Electrolytic cell, it has a non-spontaneous and endothermic reaction.#2 Similarities Cells Oxidation occurs at the anode, while reduction occurs at the cathode. ①Electrons always flow through the external circuit (wires) from the anode to the cathode.👣Baby Steps①Why ① affect?Regardless of the ❰ * ❱, the anode is always the site of electron loss, and the cathode is always the site of electron gain. 🧧Special move①Classifying directionRule : Electrons flow from negative pole to positive poleSpontaneous : Anode lose e- readily → act as negative poleNon-spontaneous : help it lose e- readily → need external to pull e- out → connected to positive pole 🤟Show FlatExplain whether both Chemical cell and Electrolytic cell have the same electrode processes. (2 marks)Yes both of them has the same electrode processes (i.e. oxidation occurs at the anode, while reduction occurs at the cathode.) , since Regardless of the type of cell, the anode is always the site of electron loss, and the cathode is always the site of electron gain. Factors affecting preferential discharge of ions (HKDSE Syllabus) 📌Major PointsFactorPosition of ions in electrochemical series [Lower (Higher) position of cations (anions), discharge more readily]Concentration of anion in solution ② [High concentration of halide ions, discharge more readily]Material of electrodes ③ [/]🎺Stroy Telling①How ① affect?If ❰ * ❱ is used as cathode, ❰ X ❱ ions instead of ❰ Y ❱ will be discharged due to the lower position in electrochemical series of ❰ X ❱How ② affect?If ❰ * ❱ is used, ❰ X ❱ ions instead of ❰ Y ❱ will be discharged due to the concentration effectHow ③ affect? If ❰ * ❱ is used anode, ❰ * ❱ will be liberated at the anode. If ❰ * ❱ is used anode, anode will dissolve.🤟Show FlatUsing the electrolysis of copper(II) chloride solution as an example, briefly discuss the factors affecting the discharge of ions in electrolysis. (9 marks)Position of ions in electrochemical series : If ❰ * ❱ is used as cathode, ❰ X ❱ ions instead of ❰ Y ❱ will be discharged due to the lower position in electrochemical series of ❰ X ❱Concentration of anion in solution : If concentrate CuCl2 is used, Cu2+ ions instead of H+ ions will be discharged due to the concentration effectMaterial of electrodes : If Carbon/Platinum is used anode, Cl2/O2 will be liberated at the anode. If Cu is used anode, anode will dissolve.(1 mark for factor + 1 mark for explanation + 1 mark for comparison + 3 marks for communication ) Factors affecting the rate of electrolysis (HKDSE Syllabus) 📌Major PointsFactorCurrent [The rate of electrolysis is directly proportional to the current flowing through the cell.]👣Baby Steps①How ① affect?A higher current means a greater number of electrons are transferred per unit time, which increases the rate at which ions migrate and discharge at the electrodes. Factors affecting the current (HKDSE Syllabus) 📌Major PointsFactorsVoltage of direct current supply [↑ voltage of d.c. supply, ↑ current] ①Distance of the the electrodes [↓ distance of the electrodes, ↑ current] ②Surface area of electrode [↑ surface area of electrodes , ↑ current] ③Concentration of solutions [↑ concentration of solution, ↑ current] ④👣Baby Steps①How ① affect?Higher voltage provides a stronger driving force to push electrons and attract ions to the electrodes and vice versa. How ② affect?Decreasing the distance between the electrodes shortens the path that ions must travel through the electrolyte, which decreases the internal resistance of the cell and vice versa.How ③ affect?Increasing the surface area of the electrodes provides more active sites for the chemical reactions to take place and vice versa. How ④ affect?A higher concentration of electrolyte means there are more mobile ions per unit volume available to carry the charge and vice versa.ConclusionThis increases the rate of migration and discharge of ions, resulting in a faster flow of electrons (i.e. higher current) through the circuit. ①②③This increases the electrical conductivity (i.e. lowers the internal resistance) of the solution, resulting in a higher current ④ Common Wordings/Questions in Electrolytic cell (HKDSE Syllabus) 📌Major Points#1 Preferential DischargeAnode/Oxidation ❰ X ❱ is a stronger reducing agent than both ❰ Y ❱ and ❰ Z ❱ ❰ X ❱ is preferentially discharge/oxidized.Cathode/Reduction ❰ X ❱ is a stronger oxidizing agent than both ❰ Y ❱ and ❰ Z ❱ ❰ X ❱ is preferentially discharge/reduced.👣Baby StepsWhy is preference not presence in chemical cells?Chemical cells rely on spontaneous redox reactions driven by the difference in the metals' tendency to lose electrons, rather than an external force. The preferential discharge of ions occurs in electrolytic cells, where an external voltage forces migrating ions to compete for electron transfer at the electrodes.Why is removal of other ions not necessary?Since they have a very low tendency to gain electrons and will not be preferentially discharged at the cathode.🤟Show FlatExplain why a chemical cell does not involve the preferential discharge of ions. Thus, keep the sign (+). Chemical Method 1 : Sampling and Titration Method (HKDSE Syllabus) 📌Major PointsMethods of QuenchingRapid cooling by putting the sample into an ice-bathDiluting with large amount of cold distilled water or other appropriate solvent Removing (killing) catalysts or certain reactants by adding an excess amount of a particular chemicalMeasurement[Reaction Time]Start the timer when mixing the solution (i.e. t = 0)Stop the timer when ❰ X ❱ turns from ❰ * ❱ to ❰ * ❱👣Baby Steps①Why is quenching necessary?To prevent making inaccurate concentration and time measurements.Why add iced water before titration?To quench (stop) the reaction immediately.By lowering the temperature and diluting the reactants, preventing further change in concentration during titration.Why take the sampling time? Once the sample is added to ice-cold water, the reaction is quenched, so the concentration of acid corresponds to that exact moment. The duration of the subsequent titration process does not affect the composition of the quenched sample. Preventing pressure buildup that inhibits gas collection.🤟Show FlatDescribe how to stop the reaction when taking out a sample for titration at a specific time. TimerTargetReaction involves a change in number of mole of gas in a closed systemPrecautionReaction vessel be strictly sealed/closed when measuring gas pressureMeasurementPressure is traced by pressure sensor connected to a data-logger.💰Examples①ExamplesCaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2, 0 mole gases → 1 mole)2NO2 + 2H2 → N2 + 2H2O (4 mole gases → 3 mole)👣Baby Steps①Why is it not suitable?Since there is no change in the total number of moles of gas, the total pressure remains constant throughout the reaction.Why vessel should strictly sealed?To maintain a fixed volume (constant volume) so that any change in the number of gas molecules directly changes the gas pressure.Why using data-logger?Allows real-time/continuous data collection Higher precision and automatic plotting of pressure vs. time graphs.🤟Show FlatDescribe how to stop the reaction when taking out a sample for titration at a specific time. Negative Catalyst (HKDSE Syllabus) 🔑Key PhrasesPositive CatalystA substance that increases the rate of reaction by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energyNegative CatalystA substance that decreases the rate of reaction by providing an alternative pathway with a higher activation energ.💰ExamplesPositive CatalystManganese(IV) oxide : Decomposition of hydrogen peroxideIron : Haber Process (synthesis of ammonia from H2 or N2Concentrated H2SO4 : Esterification of alkanoic acid and alcohol Platinum/Rhodium (Rh)/Palladium (Pd) : Catalytic converters in cars Finely divided Nickel : Hydrogenation of alkenes/unsaturated oils to form alkanes/margarineNegative CatalystPhosphoric acid (weak) : Added to concentrated hydrogen peroxide o retard its spontaneous decomposition Vitamin C/Vitamin E : Added to food systems to slow down oxidation.👣Baby Steps①Differences❰ X ❱ (i.e Positive Catalyst) increases the reaction rate while ❰ Y ❱ (i.e Negative Catalyst) decrease the reaction rate.❰ X ❱ (i.e Positive Catalyst) provides pathway with lower activation energy while ❰ Y ❱ (i.e Negative Catalyst) provides pathway with higher activation energy.❰ X ❱ (i.e Positive Catalyst) increases the frequency of effective collisions while ❰ Y ❱ (i.e Negative Catalyst) decrease the frequency of effective collisions ❰ X ❱ (i.e Positive Catalyst) increases ❰ * ❱ while ❰ Y ❱ (i.e Negative Catalyst) decrease ❰ * ❱❰ * ❱Fraction of particles with with energy equal to or greater than the lower activation energy increases.🤟Show FlatWhy is Copper melleable?
